claim: The dopamine transporter promoter is active in the neonatal striatum on postnatal day 1 (P1).
source: Consistent with early development of the dopaminergic projection from SNc/VTA to striatum, the dopamine transporter promoter is active and dopaminergic axons are found in the neonatal striatum on postnatal day 1 (P1) (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by Figure 1A showing Cre recombinase expression driven by dopamine transporter gene promoter in P1 mice.

claim: Dopaminergic axons are found in the neonatal striatum on postnatal day 1 (P1).
source: Consistent with early development of the dopaminergic projection from SNc/VTA to striatum, the dopamine transporter promoter is active and dopaminergic axons are found in the neonatal striatum on postnatal day 1 (P1) (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by Figure 1A showing densely innervating fibers within striatum at P1.

claim: By P10, the axons of midbrain dopaminergic neurons densely innervate the striatum.
source: By P10 the axons of midbrain dopaminergic neurons densely innervate the striatum and express tyrosine hydroxylase, a critical enzyme for dopamine synthesis (Figure 1B), indicating that dopaminergic neuromodulation is poised to regulate synapse and cell function during this early developmental stage.
evidence: Supported by Figure 1B showing tyrosine hydroxylase immunohistochemistry with punctate pattern in striatum at P10.

claim: By P10, dopaminergic axons in the striatum express tyrosine hydroxylase.
source: By P10 the axons of midbrain dopaminergic neurons densely innervate the striatum and express tyrosine hydroxylase, a critical enzyme for dopamine synthesis (Figure 1B), indicating that dopaminergic neuromodulation is poised to regulate synapse and cell function during this early developmental stage.
evidence: Supported by Figure 1B showing tyrosine hydroxylase expression in striatum at P10.

claim: Tyrosine hydroxylase is a critical enzyme for dopamine synthesis.
source: By P10 the axons of midbrain dopaminergic neurons densely innervate the striatum and express tyrosine hydroxylase, a critical enzyme for dopamine synthesis (Figure 1B), indicating that dopaminergic neuromodulation is poised to regulate synapse and cell function during this early developmental stage.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about tyrosine hydroxylase function.

claim: Dopaminergic neuromodulation is poised to regulate synapse and cell function during early developmental stages (P10).
source: By P10 the axons of midbrain dopaminergic neurons densely innervate the striatum and express tyrosine hydroxylase, a critical enzyme for dopamine synthesis (Figure 1B), indicating that dopaminergic neuromodulation is poised to regulate synapse and cell function during this early developmental stage.
evidence: Inferred from the presence of dopaminergic innervation and tyrosine hydroxylase expression at P10.

claim: In vivo administration of the Drd1 agonist SKF 81297 (5 mg/kg) increases dendritic spine density in dSPNs compared to saline-injected controls.
source: We observed that in acute mouse brain slices prepared 1 hr after systemic injection of the Drd1 agonist SKF 81297 (5 mg/kg), both dendritic spine density and mEPSC frequency in dSPNs were increased compared to saline-injected littermates (Figure 1C–G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing spine density of 0.29 ± 0.02 spines/µm for saline control and 0.60 ± 0.04 spines/µm for Drd1 agonist groups (p<0.001).

claim: In vivo administration of the Drd1 agonist SKF 81297 (5 mg/kg) increases mEPSC frequency in dSPNs compared to saline-injected controls.
source: We observed that in acute mouse brain slices prepared 1 hr after systemic injection of the Drd1 agonist SKF 81297 (5 mg/kg), both dendritic spine density and mEPSC frequency in dSPNs were increased compared to saline-injected littermates (Figure 1C–G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing mEPSC frequency of 593 ± 168% of control values (p<0.05).

claim: The frequency of mEPSCs in Drd1 agonist exposed dSPNs was 593 ± 168% of that in saline-treated controls.
source: The frequency of mEPSCs in Drd1 agonist exposed SPNs was 593 ± 168% of that in saline-treated controls (N = 7 and 8 neurons from 4 mice/group, Kruskal-Wallis test p = 0.0063, with p<0.05 for Dunn's multiple comparison post hoc test).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings and statistical analysis.

claim: mEPSC amplitude was not significantly different between control (10.8 ± 1.6 pA) and Drd1 agonist groups (12.7 ± 1.1 pA).
source: mEPSC amplitude was 10.8 ± 1.6 and 12.7 ± 1.1 pA for control and Drd1 agonist groups and was not significantly different (one way ANOVA, p = 0.313).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological measurements and statistical analysis.

claim: Dendritic spine density was 0.29 ± 0.02 spines/µm for saline control and 0.60 ± 0.04 spines/µm for Drd1 agonist groups.
source: Dendritic spine density was 0.29 ± 0.02 spines/µm and 0.60 ± 0.04 spines/µm for saline control and Drd1 agonist groups respectively (p<0.001 on Dunnett's multiple comparison test after one-way ANOVA; N = 36 dendrites, 12 neurons from 3 mice and 21 dendrites in 7 neurons from 3 mice).
evidence: Supported by imaging data and statistical analysis.

claim: Pretreating mice with PKA antagonist H-89 (5 mg/kg) 30 min prior to Drd1 agonist injection prevented the effects on mEPSC frequency and spine density.
source: Pretreating mice with a PKA antagonist H-89 (5 mg/kg) 30 min prior to agonist injection prevented the effects on mEPSC frequency and spine density (mEPSC frequency, 122 ± 47% of control with Drd1 agonist, N = 6 and 8 neurons from 2 mice/group, p>0.05 for Dunn's multiple comparison post hoc test; spine density, 0.27 ± 0.02 spines/µm vs. 0.29 ± 0.02 spines/µm in control and Drd1 agonist treatment conditions, N = 18 dendrites in 6 neurons from 2 mice, and 24 dendrites in 8 neurons from 2 mice).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing no significant differences when H-89 was administered.

claim: The effects of Drd1 activation on dSPN excitatory synapses suggest a PKA-dependent increase in the number of AMPA receptor-containing glutamatergic synapses.
source: These results suggest a PKA-dependent increase in the number of AMPA receptor-containing glutamatergic synapses induced by in vivo Drd1 activation.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that H-89 (PKA antagonist) prevented the effects of Drd1 agonist on mEPSC frequency and spine density.

claim: Drd1 receptor activation alone is insufficient to increase synapse number in vitro.
source: However, Drd1 receptor activation alone is insufficient to increase synapse number, as changes in mEPSC frequency or amplitude were not observed with incubation of acute brain slices in SKF 81297 in vitro (Figure 1—figure supplement 1. For mEPSC frequency, 107 ± 23% of ACSF control values with Drd1 stimulation; N = 6 neurons from 2 mice/group, t-test p = 0.83. The amplitude of mEPSCs was 12.3 ± 1.9 and 13.8 ± 2.2 pA for control and Drd1 stimulation groups respectively, t-test p = 0.51).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing no significant changes in mEPSC frequency or amplitude with in vitro Drd1 stimulation.

claim: dSPN excitatory synapse enhancement by a single, acute dose of a Drd1 receptor agonist requires intact circuitry.
source: Thus, dSPN excitatory synapse enhancement by a single, acute dose of a Drd1 receptor agonist alone requires intact circuitry, as it cannot be induced in the slice.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that in vivo Drd1 agonist treatment increased synapses but in vitro treatment did not.

claim: In vivo administration of SKF 81297 had no effects on excitatory synapses in iSPNs.
source: In contrast to the effects seen in dSPNs, in vivo administration of SKF 81297 had no effects on excitatory synapses in iSPNs (Figure 1H), consistent with the lack of expression of Drd1 receptor on these cells (Gerfen et al., 1990) (mEPSC frequency, 73.3 ± 30.1% of control values in presence of Drd1 agonist; N = 6 neurons from 4 mice and 8 neurons from 2 mice).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and citation to Gerfen et al., 1990 regarding Drd1 receptor expression.

claim: iSPNs lack expression of Drd1 receptor.
source: In contrast to the effects seen in dSPNs, in vivo administration of SKF 81297 had no effects on excitatory synapses in iSPNs (Figure 1H), consistent with the lack of expression of Drd1 receptor on these cells (Gerfen et al., 1990) (mEPSC frequency, 73.3 ± 30.1% of control values in presence of Drd1 agonist; N = 6 neurons from 4 mice and 8 neurons from 2 mice).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gerfen et al., 1990.

claim: iSPNs express Gαs-coupled Adenosine 2a (A2a) receptor, which enhances PKA activity.
source: iSPNs express Gαs-coupled Adenosine 2a (A2a) receptor, which also enhances PKA activity (Higley and Sabatini 2010) – nevertheless, administration of an agonist of A2aRs (CGS 21680, 0.1 mg/kg) had no significant effect on iSPN dendritic spine density or mEPSC rate, within the rapid time-frame of 1 hr (140 ± 63% of control, p>0.05 for control vs. A2aR agonist post-hoc comparison; N = 11 neurons from 3 mice).
evidence: Supported by citation to Higley and Sabatini 2010.

claim: Administration of A2aR agonist (CGS 21680, 0.1 mg/kg) alone had no significant effect on iSPN dendritic spine density or mEPSC rate within 1 hr.
source: iSPNs express Gαs-coupled Adenosine 2a (A2a) receptor, which also enhances PKA activity (Higley and Sabatini 2010) – nevertheless, administration of an agonist of A2aRs (CGS 21680, 0.1 mg/kg) had no significant effect on iSPN dendritic spine density or mEPSC rate, within the rapid time-frame of 1 hr (140 ± 63% of control, p>0.05 for control vs. A2aR agonist post-hoc comparison; N = 11 neurons from 3 mice).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing no significant differences.

claim: Administering Drd2 receptor agonist (quinpirole 0.5 mg/kg) resulted in no significant differences from controls in iSPNs.
source: Similarly, administering an agonist of Gαi-coupled Drd2 receptors (quinpirole 0.5 mg/kg) also resulted in no significant differences from controls (132 ± 17.0% of control, p>0.05 for control vs. Drd2 agonist post hoc comparison; N = 8 neurons from 3 mice).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing no significant differences.

claim: Co-administration of Drd1 and A2a receptor agonists increased mEPSC frequency and dendritic spine density in iSPNs, with no change in mEPSC amplitude.
source: However, co-administration of Drd1 and A2a receptor agonists increased mEPSC frequency and dendritic spine density in iSPNs, with no change in mEPSC amplitude, suggesting an increase in the number of functional excitatory synapses (Figure 1H) (mEPSC frequency, 470 ± 124% of control values with CGS 21680/SKF 81297, one-way ANOVA p<0.0008, Bonferroni post hoc p<0.05; N = 6 neurons from 4 mice and 5 neurons from 2 mice for this comparison. Dendritic spine density, 0.29 ± 0.02 spines/µm and 0.63 ± 0.05 spines/µm, for control vs. CGS 21680/SKF 81297, one-way ANOVA p<0.0001, Bonferroni post hoc p<0.0001; 31 dendrites, 9 neurons, 2 mice, and 7 dendrites, 4 neurons in 2 mice, for this comparison).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing significant increases in mEPSC frequency and spine density.

claim: Co-administration of Drd1 and A2a receptor agonists suggests an increase in the number of functional excitatory synapses in iSPNs.
source: However, co-administration of Drd1 and A2a receptor agonists increased mEPSC frequency and dendritic spine density in iSPNs, with no change in mEPSC amplitude, suggesting an increase in the number of functional excitatory synapses (Figure 1H) (mEPSC frequency, 470 ± 124% of control values with CGS 21680/SKF 81297, one-way ANOVA p<0.0008, Bonferroni post hoc p<0.05; N = 6 neurons from 4 mice and 5 neurons from 2 mice for this comparison. Dendritic spine density, 0.29 ± 0.02 spines/µm and 0.63 ± 0.05 spines/µm, for control vs. CGS 21680/SKF 81297, one-way ANOVA p<0.0001, Bonferroni post hoc p<0.0001; 31 dendrites, 9 neurons, 2 mice, and 7 dendrites, 4 neurons in 2 mice, for this comparison).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that mEPSC frequency and spine density increased without changes in amplitude.

claim: Neither the activation of dopamine receptors, nor of Gαs-coupled GPCRs, is sufficient to cell-autonomously enhance glutamatergic synapses on SPNs.
source: These results indicate that neither the activation of dopamine receptors, nor of Gαs-coupled GPCRs, is sufficient to cell-autonomously enhance glutamatergic synapses on SPNs.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that A2aR agonist alone did not increase synapses in iSPNs, but co-administration with Drd1 agonist did.

claim: Neuromodulatory GPCR signaling may be a permissive, or facilitating, signal that acts in concert with other stimuli to induce synaptogenesis in vivo.
source: Instead, neuromodulatory GPCR signaling may be a permissive, or facilitating, signal that acts in concert with other stimuli to induce synaptogenesis in vivo.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that GPCR activation alone was insufficient but combined with other signals was effective.

claim: GPCR activation modulates glutamate-induced, activity-dependent synaptogenesis.
source: We hypothesized that GPCR activation modulates glutamate-induced, activity-dependent synaptogenesis.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their observations.

claim: Drd1 activation increases dSPN excitability.
source: Since Drd1 activation also increases dSPN excitability, which in turn may increase recurrent corticostriatal glutamatergic transmission onto SPNs by altering cortical activity (Oldenburg and Sabatini, 2015), then activation of this receptor alone in vivo will (1) activate PKA and (2) enhance glutamate release.
evidence: Stated as a known fact in the context of the discussion.

claim: Drd1 activation may increase recurrent corticostriatal glutamatergic transmission onto SPNs by altering cortical activity.
source: Since Drd1 activation also increases dSPN excitability, which in turn may increase recurrent corticostriatal glutamatergic transmission onto SPNs by altering cortical activity (Oldenburg and Sabatini, 2015), then activation of this receptor alone in vivo will (1) activate PKA and (2) enhance glutamate release.
evidence: Supported by citation to Oldenburg and Sabatini, 2015.

claim: Activation of Drd1 receptor alone in vivo will activate PKA and enhance glutamate release.
source: Since Drd1 activation also increases dSPN excitability, which in turn may increase recurrent corticostriatal glutamatergic transmission onto SPNs by altering cortical activity (Oldenburg and Sabatini, 2015), then activation of this receptor alone in vivo will (1) activate PKA and (2) enhance glutamate release.
evidence: Inferred from the known effects of Drd1 activation on excitability and circuit activity.

claim: Drd1 receptor activation induces locomotion in P8-13 pups, which normally show limited mobility.
source: Such stimulatory effects of dopamine on basal ganglia circuitry are consistent with the observation of Drd1 receptor activation-induced locomotion observed in pups, which normally show limited mobility at P8-13 (Dehorter et al., 2011; Wills et al., 2014) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and citations to Dehorter et al., 2011 and Wills et al., 2014.

claim: P8-13 pups normally show limited mobility.
source: Such stimulatory effects of dopamine on basal ganglia circuitry are consistent with the observation of Drd1 receptor activation-induced locomotion observed in pups, which normally show limited mobility at P8-13 (Dehorter et al., 2011; Wills et al., 2014) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dehorter et al., 2011 and Wills et al., 2014.

claim: Priming with Drd1 receptor agonist administration at P9 potentiated agonist-evoked locomotion at P11.
source: This acute locomotion induction has lasting consequences for behavior and brain development, since priming with Drd1 receptor agonist administration at P9 potentiated agonist-evoked locomotion at P11 (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: iSPN activity is negatively coupled to intrastriatal glutamate release in the adult, via regulation of cortical activity.
source: In contrast to dSPNs, iSPNs would be expected to have more complex requirements for synaptogenesis, since iSPN activity is negatively coupled to intrastriatal glutamate release in the adult, via regulation of cortical activity (Oldenburg and Sabatini, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Oldenburg and Sabatini, 2015.

claim: The cooperation of presynaptic glutamate release and postsynaptic PKA signaling explains why coincident activation of Drd1 receptors and A2aRs is required in vivo to increase synaptogenesis in iSPNs.
source: We hypothesize that the cooperation of presynaptic glutamate release and postsynaptic PKA signaling explains why coincident activation of Drd1 receptors (to recurrently drive glutamate release) and A2aRs (to enhance PKA signaling) is required in vivo to increase synaptogenesis in iSPNs.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors to explain their observations.

claim: Spatio-temporally controlled glutamate release can focally and rapidly induce de novo formation of a synapse-bearing dendritic spine on young cortical pyramidal neurons.
source: Spatio-temporally controlled glutamate release can focally and rapidly induce de novo formation of a synapse-bearing dendritic spine on young cortical pyramidal neurons (Kwon and Sabatini, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kwon and Sabatini, 2011.

claim: Repeated glutamate uncaging (40 pulses at 2 Hz) with pulse durations of 0.5–4 ms induced de novo growth of a dendritic spine-like protrusion in a subset of cases.
source: Repeated glutamate uncaging (40 pulses at 2 Hz) with a variety of pulse durations (0.5–4 ms) was applied near a GFP-positive dendrite under conditions that maximally activate NMDA-type glutamate receptors (0 mM added extracellular Mg2+). In a subset of cases, this protocol induced de novo growth of a dendritic spine-like protrusion (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and Figure 2C showing spine formation.

claim: De novo spinogenesis occurred at proximal uncaging locations (<2 µm from dendrite) but not at distal locations (>5 µm away).
source: As a control for non-specific, photodamage-induced changes in tissue fluorescence, in a subset of trials, an interleaved stimulus of identical strength was delivered to a control site >5 µm away from any labeled dendrite (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1) (0.5 vs. 0 success probability at proximal and distal uncaging locations; 82 trials from 2 mice).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing 0.5 vs. 0 success probability at proximal and distal locations.

claim: P8-13 SPNs of both pathways were capable of de novo spinogenesis in response to glutamate uncaging.
source: As was previously described for layer 2/3 pyramidal neurons, P8-13 SPNs of both pathways were capable of de novo spinogenesis in response to glutamate uncaging (Kozorovitskiy et al., 2012; Kwon and Sabatini, 2011).
evidence: Supported by experimental observations and citations to previous studies.

claim: The basal rate of spinogenesis and its dependence on uncaging pulse width and proximity to the dendrite were similar for striatal SPNs and previously examined cortical neurons.
source: The basal rate of spinogenesis (the probability of induction of a structure shaped like a dendritic spine), as well as its dependence on uncaging pulse width and proximity to the dendrite were similar for striatal SPNs and previously examined cortical neurons (Kwon and Sabatini, 2011).
evidence: Supported by comparison to previous study by Kwon and Sabatini, 2011.

claim: For both dSPNs and iSPNs, the success rate for spinogenesis inductions with stimulation 1–2 µm away from a labeled dendrite was ~20–50%, with longer uncaging pulses associated with a greater probability of spinogenesis.
source: For both dSPNs and iSPNs, the success rate for inductions with stimulation 1–2 µm away from a labeled dendrite was ~20–50%, with longer uncaging pulses associated with a greater probability of spinogenesis (dSPNs, N = 146 and 174 trials in 10 mice for control group and in presence of GPCR agonist, respectively, balanced across conditions; iSPNs, N = 132 and 164 trials in 11 mice).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from multiple trials.

claim: The probability of spinogenesis increased in the presence of SKF 81297 for dSPNs.
source: The probability of spinogenesis increased in the presence of SKF 81297 for dSPNs, and CGS 21680 for iSPNs, respectively (the proportion of success trials was 0.23, 0.40, and 0.57 in the control condition, for varied length glutamate uncaging pulses, and 0.44, 0.62, and 0.76 in presence of Drd1 receptor agonist for dSPNs; for iSPNs, the respective proportions were 0.19, 0.46, and 0.49 in the control condition vs. 0.73, 0.74, and 0.70 for iSPNs with A2aR stimulation; two-tailed Z tests for proportions, p = 0.040, 0.015, and 0.018 for dSPNs, and p<0.0001, p = 0.018, and 0.008 for iSPNs).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: The probability of spinogenesis increased in the presence of CGS 21680 for iSPNs.
source: The probability of spinogenesis increased in the presence of SKF 81297 for dSPNs, and CGS 21680 for iSPNs, respectively (the proportion of success trials was 0.23, 0.40, and 0.57 in the control condition, for varied length glutamate uncaging pulses, and 0.44, 0.62, and 0.76 in presence of Drd1 receptor agonist for dSPNs; for iSPNs, the respective proportions were 0.19, 0.46, and 0.49 in the control condition vs. 0.73, 0.74, and 0.70 for iSPNs with A2aR stimulation; two-tailed Z tests for proportions, p = 0.040, 0.015, and 0.018 for dSPNs, and p<0.0001, p = 0.018, and 0.008 for iSPNs).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: Gαs-coupled receptor stimulation decreased the number of glutamate pulses necessary to induce spinogenesis.
source: Analysis of the time course of spine formation for successful inductions reveals that Gαs-coupled receptor stimulation decreased the number of glutamate pulses necessary to induce spinogenesis (Figure 2F).
evidence: Supported by analysis of time course data in Figure 2F.

claim: Spine growth occurs rapidly in all conditions, as observed in pyramidal neurons.
source: Whereas spine growth occurs rapidly in all conditions, as observed in pyramidal neurons (Kwon and Sabatini, 2011), SKF 81297 and CGS 21680 accelerated the onset of spinogenesis for dSPNs and iSPNs, respectively.
evidence: Supported by experimental observations and citation to Kwon and Sabatini, 2011.

claim: SKF 81297 and CGS 21680 accelerated the onset of spinogenesis for dSPNs and iSPNs, respectively.
source: Whereas spine growth occurs rapidly in all conditions, as observed in pyramidal neurons (Kwon and Sabatini, 2011), SKF 81297 and CGS 21680 accelerated the onset of spinogenesis for dSPNs and iSPNs, respectively.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing reduced number of pulses to threshold.

claim: At 2 Hz stimulation, for successful trials, threshold pulse number was 21.3 without drug and 6.0 in the presence of Gαs agonist for dSPNs.
source: At 2 Hz stimulation, for successful trials, threshold pulse number was 21.3 without drug and 6.0 in the presence of Gαs agonist for dSPNs, and 17.4 vs. 8.7 pulses for iSPNs (Mann-Whitney test, p = 0.0025 and p = 0.0048 for d- and iSPN comparisons, respectively; N = 12 and 13 induction trials for dSPN control vs. in the presence of agonist, with 16 and 17 induction trials for iSPNs, respectively).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: At 2 Hz stimulation, for successful trials, threshold pulse number was 17.4 without drug and 8.7 in the presence of Gαs agonist for iSPNs.
source: At 2 Hz stimulation, for successful trials, threshold pulse number was 21.3 without drug and 6.0 in the presence of Gαs agonist for dSPNs, and 17.4 vs. 8.7 pulses for iSPNs (Mann-Whitney test, p = 0.0025 and p = 0.0048 for d- and iSPN comparisons, respectively; N = 12 and 13 induction trials for dSPN control vs. in the presence of agonist, with 16 and 17 induction trials for iSPNs, respectively).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: Cell-autonomous mechanisms exist for neuromodulatory regulation of glutamate-dependent spinogenesis.
source: Given that glutamate was exogenously controlled and Gαs receptors were stimulated by agonist bath application, these findings suggest the presence of cell-autonomous mechanisms for neuromodulatory regulation of glutamate-dependent spinogenesis.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental design where glutamate and receptor activation were controlled exogenously.

claim: If a similar interaction of neuromodulation and glutamate release controls synapse formation in vivo, it should be possible to bias rapidly developing networks towards increased synaptogenesis by briefly enhancing either PKA signaling or glutamate release.
source: If a similar interaction of neuromodulation and glutamate release controls synapse formation in vivo, it should be possible to bias rapidly developing networks towards increased synaptogenesis by briefly enhancing either PKA signaling or glutamate release.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the hypothesis of cooperative neuromodulation and glutamate signaling.

claim: Rs1 is a modified Gαs-coupled GPCR sensitive to a small, exogenous, blood-brain-barrier permeable ligand.
source: To test this prediction for PKA signaling, we used a pharmacogenetic approach based on Rs1, a modified Gαs-coupled GPCR sensitive to a small, exogenous, blood-brain-barrier permeable ligand (Srinivasan et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Srinivasan et al., 2003.

claim: Rs1 has a sub-micromolar EC50 of activation.
source: Transfection of HEK293 cells with Rs1, followed by incubation in the agonist RS 67333 and chemi-luminescent analysis of SEAP levels revealed a sub-micromolar EC50 of Rs1 activation (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by SEAP assay data in Figure 3A.

claim: Light-evoked EPSC amplitude was increased in virally transduced SPNs expressing Rs1, compared to control hemisphere SPNs.
source: Consistent with our hypothesis, light-evoked EPSC amplitude was increased in virally transduced SPNs, compared to control hemisphere SPNs (Figure 3G; light-evoked EPSC amplitude, 68.6 ± 29.9 pA control vs. 150.3 ± 55.8 pA injected hemisphere; N = 21 and 23 neurons from 4 mice/group, t-test p = 0.039).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data and statistical analysis.

claim: In vivo transient activation of a Gαs-coupled GPCR in SPNs is sufficient to rapidly enhance corticostriatal connectivity.
source: Thus, in vivo transient activation of a Gαs-coupled GPCR in SPNs is sufficient to rapidly enhance corticostriatal connectivity, in the presence of otherwise normal corticostriatal transmission.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Rs1 activation increased light-evoked EPSCs.

claim: The observed sufficiency of pharmacogenetic PKA activation to enhance corticostriatal connectivity for iSPNs stems from the likelihood that concurrent pharmacogenetic activation of Gαs cascades in dSPNs enhances corticostriatal glutamatergic drive via recurrent connections.
source: The observed sufficiency of pharmacogenetic PKA activation to enhance corticostriatal connectivity for iSPNs (in contrast to stimulating iSPNs with an A2aR agonist, as in Figure 1H) stems from the likelihood that the concurrent pharmacogenetic activation of Gαs cascades in dSPNs enhances corticostriatal glutamatergic drive via recurrent connections and regulating cortical activity (Oldenburg and Sabatini, 2015).
evidence: Inferred from the experimental design and supported by citation to Oldenburg and Sabatini, 2015.

claim: In vivo optogenetic stimulation of cortex (300 pulses of light over 1 hr) induced moderate c-fos expression in the stimulated cortical region.
source: Mice were awake and freely moving within an enclosure, when a mild stimulus was delivered, consisting of 300 pulses of light over the course of 1 hr, given in bursts of 5 pulses at 20 Hz every minute (Figure 4A). This treatment induced moderate c-fos expression in the stimulated cortical region (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemical data in Figure 4B.

claim: In vivo optogenetic stimulation of cortex increased both EPSC peak amplitude and charge transfer in SPNs on the stimulated side.
source: Both EPSC peak amplitude and charge transfer were increased on the stimulated side (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1) (Light-evoked EPSC amplitude, 30.5 ± 4.8 pA vs. 50.4 ± 6.6 pA for control and stimulated hemisphere comparison; charge transfer, 0.32 ± 0.14 pC and 0.89 ± 0.21 pC; N = 29–33 neurons/group, 4 mice/group).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data and statistical analysis.

claim: Paired analysis of EPSC amplitude within subjects across the two hemispheres confirms successful induction of corticostriatal rewiring following cortical optogenetic stimulation.
source: Paired analysis of EPSC amplitude within subjects across the two hemispheres is consistent with individual cell data (Figure 4D), confirming the successful induction of corticostriatal rewiring following cortical optogenetic stimulation (EPSC amplitude, control 16.2 ± 3.2 vs. 27.3 ± 3.2 pA in the stimulated hemisphere, paired t-test p = 0.026, 4 mice/group).
evidence: Supported by paired statistical analysis of electrophysiological data.

claim: A major component of the functional reorganization induced through brief in vivo stimulation of corticostriatal afferents in young mice is locally expressed in the striatum.
source: These data demonstrate that a major component of the functional reorganization induced through brief in vivo stimulation of corticostriatal afferents in young mice is locally expressed in the striatum.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that effects persisted in striatum-only slices with cortex removed.

claim: Optogenetically induced corticostriatal plasticity was blocked by pre-administration of PKA inhibitor H-89 (5 mg/kg).
source: We further probed the pharmacological dependence of this form of plasticity and found that it was blocked by either pre-administration of PKA inhibitor H-89 (5 mg/kg), or by a combination of Drd1 and A2aR blockers SKF 83566 (0.5 mg/kg) and istradefylline/KW-6002 (2.5 mg/kg), administered 30 min before optogenetic stimulation (Figure 4F–G). Light-evoked EPSC amplitude, in presence of H-89, was 18.8 ± 4.4 pA vs. 13.8 ± 3.3 pA in neurons from control and stimulated hemispheres (t-test p = 0.376, N = 22 and 19 neurons from 3 mice/group).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing no significant differences with H-89 treatment.

claim: SPN changes induced by glutamatergic stimulation require PKA signaling, which is activated via Drd1 and A2aR for dSPNs and iSPNs, respectively.
source: Thus, SPN changes induced by glutamatergic stimulation require PKA signaling, which in turn is activated via Drd1 and A2aR for dSPNs and iSPNs, respectively.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that PKA and receptor blockers prevented optogenetically induced plasticity.

claim: Increasing either pre-synaptic glutamatergic drive or enhancing striatal PKA signaling is sufficient to rapidly alter SPN synaptogenesis.
source: Increasing either pre-synaptic glutamatergic drive or enhancing striatal PKA signaling is sufficient to rapidly alter SPN synaptogenesis, supporting the idea of cooperative, neuromodulation-dependent circuit remodeling during striatal development.
evidence: Inferred from the combined results of pharmacogenetic and optogenetic experiments.

claim: The same optogenetic stimulation parameters that evoked PKA-dependent enhancements in evoked responses in vivo were sufficient to produce a moderate enhancement in light-evoked corticostriatal responses in vitro.
source: We found that the same optogenetic stimulation parameters that evoked PKA-dependent enhancements in evoked responses in vivo were sufficient to produce a moderate enhancement in light-evoked corticostriatal responses in vitro.
evidence: Supported by ex vivo optogenetic stimulation experiments.

claim: In ex vivo experiments, the amplitude of evoked responses was 528.8 ± 69 pA for control and 694.4 ± 79 pA for stimulated slices.
source: In experiments using within-mouse controls, the amplitude of evoked responses was 528.8 ± 69 pA and 694.4 ± 79 pA, for neurons in control and stimulated slices respectively (Figure 5B–C) (Mann-Whitney test, p = 0.037, N = 64 and 61 neurons from 4 mice).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data and statistical analysis.

claim: Incubation in PKA agonists alone was insufficient to alter evoked response amplitude in vitro.

claim: PKA activity, via Gαs GPCRs, generally serves to potentiate activity-dependent synaptogenesis during the time of rapid synapse production.
source: The observation that two types of Gαs-dependent modulation appear to regulate synaptogenesis in d- and iSPNs raises the possibility that PKA activity, via Gαs GPCRs, generally serves to potentiate activity-dependent synaptogenesis during the time of rapid synapse production.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation that both Drd1 and A2aR (both Gαs-coupled) enhance synaptogenesis.

claim: The array of Gαs GPCRs expressed in the central nervous system is substantial and includes abundant receptors such as 5-HT4 and 5-HT7 serotonin receptors, beta-adrenergic receptors, and corticotropin-releasing factor receptors.
source: The array of Gαs GPCRs expressed in the central nervous system is substantial and includes abundant receptors such as 5-HT4 and 5-HT7 serotonin receptors (Giulietti et al., 2014), as well beta-adrenergic (Nomura et al., 2014; Arriza et al., 1992) and corticotropin-releasing factor receptors (Fu and Neugebauer, 2008; Riegel and Williams, 2008).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to studies identifying these receptors.

claim: A general role for neuromodulators acting on Gαs GPCRs during neural circuit development would transform our understanding of core principles in developmental neurobiology.
source: A general role for neuromodulators acting on Gαs GPCRs during neural circuit development would transform our understanding of core principles in developmental neurobiology, greatly expanding the list therapeutic targets for neurodevelopmental and neurodegenerative disorders.
evidence: This is speculation about the broader implications of the findings.

claim: Dopamine performs critical functions in motivated, goal-directed learning and behavior in the vertebrate basal ganglia.

claim: Classical models propose that the activity of dopamine-producing neurons encodes reward prediction errors.

evidence: Based on established models in the field.

claim: Direct and indirect pathways are comprised of two classes of striatal spiny projection output neurons that express different types of dopamine receptors.
source: An important element of this model is the distinct action of dopamine on the direct and indirect pathways, comprised of two classes of striatal spiny projection output neurons that express different types of dopamine receptors, project to separate downstream targets, and regulate complementary aspects of motor behavior (Bateup et al., 2010; Kravitz et al., 2010; Cui et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bateup et al., 2010; Kravitz et al., 2010; Cui et al., 2013.

evidence: Supported by citation to Kozorovitskiy et al., 2012.
